title: XVI-XXI: absolute and conditioned; antecedent and consequent
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): by means belonging toward consequent will confers righteousness on believers plus inflicts eternal death on ye impenitent — so God by means belonging toward antecedent will wants all men to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). by means belonging toward consequent will some to die toward crimes; — this can be called judicial will — as a magistrate by means belonging toward antecedent will wants all citizens alive. circumstances being posited, He wills — consequent that same by means belonging toward which. Antecedent will stands as that same by means belonging toward that same which God wills something before particular circumstances stand as considered; FOURTH, God's will stands as antecedent or consequent. XIX. Conditioned stands as that same by means belonging toward that same which God wills something under a condition. XVIII. Absolute stands as that same by means belonging toward that same which God wills something without condition. XVII. THIRD, God's will stands as absolute or conditioned. XVI.
pass_b_english: XVI. THIRD, God's will is absolute or conditioned. XVII. Absolute is that by which God wills something without condition. XVIII. Conditioned is that by which God wills something under a condition. XIX. FOURTH, God's will is antecedent or consequent.

Antecedent will is that by which God wills something before particular circumstances are considered; consequent that by which, circumstances being posited, He wills. This can be called judicial will — as a magistrate by antecedent will wants all citizens alive, by consequent will some to die for crimes; so God by antecedent will wants all men to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), by consequent will confers righteousness on believers and inflicts eternal death on the impenitent.
source_text: XVI. TERTIO, voluntas Dei est absoluta aut conditionata. XVII. Absoluta est qua Deus aliquid vult sine conditione. XVIII. Conditionata est qua Deus aliquid vult sub conditione. XIX. QUARTO, voluntas Dei est antecedens aut consequens. Voluntas antecedens est qua Deus vult aliquid priusquam considerentur circumstantiae particulares; consequens qua, positis circumstantiis, vult. Haec dici potest voluntas judiciaria — sicut magistratus voluntate antecedente vult omnes cives vivos esse, consequente aliquos mori propter scelera; sic Deus voluntate antecedente vult omnes homines salvos fieri, I Tim. II.4, voluntate consequente credentibus justitiam confert, impoenitentibus mortem aeternam infligit.
